title: Car insurance customers slugged for loyalty: ASIC
full_text:
The corporate regulator says not a single insurer is properly explaining to customers why car policy premiums are rising or how they're calculated, making it difficult to compare options.
The Australian Securities and Investments Commission raised its concerns as it increases scrutiny on insurance companies over pricing amid a rapid increase in premiums. The regulator said it was particularly concerned that poor disclosures meant customers were paying "a price for loyalty".
Insurance is the most-complained-about product across the entire financial services industry, and car insurance is the most problematic area.
"We think insurers can do a lot more to explain the reasons for premium increases, and particularly when people are facing significant increases that go beyond the rate of inflation," ASIC commissioner Alan Kirkland said.
The criticism of car insurance policies comes ahead of earnings updates this week from the three major providers: Suncorp, IAG and QBE Insurance.
Motor vehicle insurance premiums rose 8 per cent in the 12 months to July last year after increasing more than 42 per cent between 2019 and 2024, but ASIC found insurers provided only generic explanations for increases, while some provided no explanation at all.
"When people see big increases, then their expectations for an explanation are a lot higher, and that's perfectly understandable," Kirkland said.
"Insurers should be explaining the key factors that are fed into a premium and into a premium increase in terms that people can understand. These should also be prominently displayed on the quote and renewal documents, so people don't have to go digging around in supporting material to find it."
In the May budget, the Albanese government committed to consider changes that would force insurer to be clearer in pricing decision.
The Financial Rights Legal Centre and other consumer groups said on Tuesday that this "must lead to strong legal requirements on insurers to provide their customers with a breakdown of the key components of their premium and a tailored explanation of why their premium has increased".
ASIC's review of eight insurance brands across five insurers - around 72 per cent of the market - and a survey of more than 2000 consumers found loyal customers who hadn't challenged their premium were paying more.
Of those who did contact their insurer before renewing, 31 per cent secured a lower premium without changing their policy settings. But without detailed reasoning about the drivers of cost, it was "harder for people to push back, and know whether they might want to challenge the reason," Kirkland said.
